Content:
(a) Computation of amount

From the sums appropriated therefor, the Secretary (except as otherwise provided in this section) shall pay to each State which has a plan approved under this subchapter, for each quarter, beginning with the quarter commencing January 1, 1966—

(1) an amount equal to the Federal medical assistance percentage (as defined in section 1396d(b) of this title, subject to subsections (g) and (j) of this section and section 1396r–4(f) of this title) of the total amount expended during such quarter as medical assistance under the State plan; plus

(2)(A) an amount equal to 75 per centum of so much of the sums expended during such quarter (as found necessary by the Secretary for the proper and efficient administration of the State plan) as are attributable to compensation or training of skilled professional medical personnel, and staff directly supporting such personnel, of the State agency or any other public agency; plus

(B) notwithstanding paragraph (1) or subparagraph (A), with respect to amounts expended for nursing aide training and competency evaluation programs, and competency evaluation programs, described in section 1396r(e)(1) of this title (including the costs for nurse aides to complete such competency evaluation programs), regardless of whether the programs are provided in or outside nursing facilities or of the skill of the personnel involved in such programs, an amount equal to 50 percent (or, for calendar quarters beginning on or after July 1, 1988, and before October 1, 1990, the lesser of 90 percent or the Federal medical assistance percentage plus 25 percentage points) of so much of the sums expended during such quarter (as found necessary by the Secretary for the proper and efficient administration of the State plan) as are attributable to such programs; plus

(C) an amount equal to 75 percent of so much of the sums expended during such quarter (as found necessary by the Secretary for the proper and efficient administration of the State plan) as are attributable to preadmission screening and resident review activities conducted by the State under section 1396r(e)(7) of this title; plus

(D) for each calendar quarter during—

(i) fiscal year 1991, an amount equal to 90 percent,

(ii) fiscal year 1992, an amount equal to 85 percent,

(iii) fiscal year 1993, an amount equal to 80 percent, and

(iv) fiscal year 1994 and thereafter, an amount equal to 75 percent,

of so much of the sums expended during such quarter (as found necessary by the Secretary for the proper and efficient administration of the State plan) as are attributable to State activities under section 1396r(g) of this title; plus

(E) an amount equal to 75 percent of so much of the sums expended during such quarter (as found necessary by the Secretary for the proper and efficient administration of the State plan) as are attributable to translation or interpretation services in connection with the enrollment of, retention of, and use of services under this subchapter by, children of families for whom English is not the primary language; plus

(3) an amount equal to—

(A)(i) 90 per centum of so much of the sums expended during such quarter as are attributable to the design, development, or installation of such mechanized claims processing and information retrieval systems as the Secretary determines are likely to provide more efficient, economical, and effective administration of the plan and to be compatible with the claims processing and information retrieval systems utilized in the administration of subchapter XVIII, including the State's share of the cost of installing such a system to be used jointly in the administration of such State's plan and the plan of any other State approved under this subchapter,

Title: Section 1915(l). State plan amendment option to provide medical assistance for certain individuals who are patients in certain institutions for mental diseases
Section: 1915(l)
Policy: SSA-Title-19
Type: federal_statute
Citation link: [Social Security Act — Title XIX (Medicaid)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)

Content:
(l) State plan amendment option to provide medical assistance for certain individuals who are patients in certain institutions for mental diseases

(1) In general

With respect to calendar quarters beginning on or after October 1, 2019, a State may elect, through a State plan amendment, to provide medical assistance for items and services furnished to an eligible individual who is a patient in an eligible institution for mental diseases in accordance with the requirements of this subsection.

(2) Payments

Subject to paragraphs (3) and (4), amounts expended under a State plan amendment under paragraph (1) for services described in such paragraph furnished, with respect to a 12-month period, to an eligible individual who is a patient in an eligible institution for mental diseases shall be treated as medical assistance for which payment is made under section 1396b(a) of this title but only to the extent that such services are furnished for not more than a period of 30 days (whether or not consecutive) during such 12-month period.

(3) Maintenance of effort

(A) In general

As a condition for a State receiving payments under section 1396b(a) of this title for medical assistance provided in accordance with this subsection, the State shall (during the period in which it so furnished such medical assistance through a State plan amendment under this subsection) maintain on an annual basis a level of funding expended by the State (and political subdivisions thereof) from non-Federal funds for items and services (including services described in subparagraph (B)) furnished to eligible individuals in outpatient and community-based settings that is not less than the level of such funding for such items and services for, at the option of the State—

(i) fiscal year 2018; or

(ii) the most recently ended fiscal year as of the date the State submits a State plan amendment to the Secretary to provide such medical assistance in accordance with this subsection.

(B) Services described

For purposes of subparagraph (A), services described in this subparagraph are the following:

(i) Outpatient and community-based substance use disorder treatment.

(ii) Evidence-based recovery and support services.

(iii) Clinically-directed therapeutic treatment to facilitate recovery skills, relapse prevention, and emotional coping strategies.

(iv) Outpatient medication-assisted treatment, related therapies, and pharmacology.

(v) Counseling and clinical monitoring.

(vi) Outpatient withdrawal management and related treatment designed to alleviate acute emotional, behavioral, cognitive, or biomedical distress resulting from, or occurring with, an individual's use of alcohol and other drugs.

(vii) Routine monitoring of medication adherence.

(viii) Other outpatient and community-based services for the treatment of substance use disorders, as designated by the Secretary.

(C) State reporting requirement

(i) In general

Prior to approval of a State plan amendment under this subsection, as a condition for a State receiving payments under section 1396b(a) of this title for medical assistance provided in accordance with this subsection, the State shall report to the Secretary, in accordance with the process established by the Secretary under clause (ii), the information deemed necessary by the Secretary under such clause.

(ii) Process

Not later than the date that is 8 months after October 24, 2018, the Secretary shall establish a process for States to report to the Secretary, at such time and in such manner as the Secretary deems appropriate, such information as the Secretary deems necessary to verify a State's compliance with subparagraph (A).

(D) Application of maintenance of effort requirements to certain States

In the case of a State with a State plan amendment in effect on September 30, 2023, for the 1-year period beginning on March 9, 2024, the provisions of subparagraph (A) shall be applied as if the amendments to such subparagraph made by the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024 had never been made.

(4) Ensuring a continuum of services

(A) In general

As a condition for a State receiving payments under section 1396b(a) of this title for medical assistance provided in accordance with this subsection, the State shall carry out each of the requirements described in subparagraphs (B) through (F).

(B) Notification

The State shall have in place evidence-based, substance use disorder-specific individual placement criteria and utilization management approaches to ensure placement of eligible individuals in an appropriate level of care, including criteria and approaches to ensure that eligible individuals receive appropriate evidence-based clinical screening prior to being furnished with items and services in an eligible institution for mental diseases, including initial and periodic assessments to determine the appropriate level of care, length of stay, and setting for such care for each individual. The State shall notify the Secretary at such time and in such form and manner as the Secretary shall require of such criteria and utilization management approaches.

(C) Outpatient services; inpatient and residential services

(i) Outpatient services

The State shall, at a minimum, provide medical assistance for services that could otherwise be covered under the State plan, consistent with each of the following outpatient levels of care:

(I) Early intervention for individuals who, for a known reason, are at risk of developing substance-related problems and for individuals for whom there is not yet sufficient information to document a diagnosable substance use disorder.

(II) Outpatient services for less than 9 hours per week for adults, and for less than 6 hours per week for adolescents, for recovery or motivational enhancement therapies and strategies.

(III) Intensive outpatient services for 9 hours or more per week for adults, and for 6 hours or more per week for adolescents, to treat multidimensional instability.

(m) "Medicaid managed care organization" defined; duties and functions of Secretary; payments to States; reporting requirements; remedies

(1)(A) The term "medicaid managed care organization" means a health maintenance organization, an eligible organization with a contract under section 1395mm of this title or a Medicare+Choice organization with a contract under part C of subchapter XVIII, a provider sponsored organization, or any other public or private organization, which meets the requirement of section 1396a(w) of this title and—

(i) makes services it provides to individuals eligible for benefits under this subchapter accessible to such individuals, within the area served by the organization, to the same extent as such services are made accessible to individuals (eligible for medical assistance under the State plan) not enrolled with the organization, and

(ii) has made adequate provision against the risk of insolvency, which provision is satisfactory to the State, meets the requirements of subparagraph (C)(i) (if applicable), and which assures that individuals eligible for benefits under this subchapter are in no case held liable for debts of the organization in case of the organization's insolvency.

An organization that is a qualified health maintenance organization (as defined in section 300e–9(d) 4 of this title) is deemed to meet the requirements of clauses (i) and (ii).

(B) The duties and functions of the Secretary, insofar as they involve making determinations as to whether an organization is a medicaid managed care organization within the meaning of subparagraph (A), shall be integrated with the administration of section 300e–11(a) and (b) of this title.

(C)(i) Subject to clause (ii), a provision meets the requirements of this subparagraph for an organization if the organization meets solvency standards established by the State for private health maintenance organizations or is licensed or certified by the State as a risk-bearing entity.

(ii) Clause (i) shall not apply to an organization if—

(I) the organization is not responsible for the provision (directly or through arrangements with providers of services) of inpatient hospital services and physicians' services;

(II) the organization is a public entity;

(III) the solvency of the organization is guaranteed by the State; or

(IV) the organization is (or is controlled by) one or more Federally-qualified health centers and meets solvency standards established by the State for such an organization.

For purposes of subclause (IV), the term "control" means the possession, whether direct or indirect, of the power to direct or cause the direction of the management and policies of the organization through membership, board representation, or an ownership interest equal to or greater than 50.1 percent.

(2)(A) Except as provided in subparagraphs (B), (C), and (G), no payment shall be made under this subchapter to a State with respect to expenditures incurred by it for payment (determined under a prepaid capitation basis or under any other risk basis) for services provided by any entity (including a health insuring organization) which is responsible for the provision (directly or through arrangements with providers of services) of inpatient hospital services and any other service described in paragraph (2), (3), (4), (5), or (7) of section 1396d(a) of this title or for the provision of any three or more of the services described in such paragraphs unless—

Content:
(kk) Provider and supplier screening, oversight, and reporting requirements

For purposes of subsection (a)(77), the requirements of this subsection are the following:

(1) Screening

(A) In general

The State complies with the process for screening providers and suppliers under this subchapter, as established by the Secretary under section 1395cc(j)(2) of this title.

(B) Provider screening against Death Master File

Beginning January 1, 2028, as part of the enrollment (or reenrollment or revalidation of enrollment) of a provider or supplier under this subchapter, and not less frequently than quarterly during the period that such provider or supplier is so enrolled, the State conducts a check of the Death Master File (as such term is defined in section 1306c(d) of this title) to determine whether such provider or supplier is deceased.

(2) Provisional period of enhanced oversight for new providers and suppliers

The State complies with procedures to provide for a provisional period of enhanced oversight for new providers and suppliers under this subchapter, as established by the Secretary under section 1395cc(j)(3) of this title.

(3) Disclosure requirements

The State requires providers and suppliers under the State plan or under a waiver of the plan to comply with the disclosure requirements established by the Secretary under section 1395cc(j)(5) of this title.

(4) Temporary moratorium on enrollment of new providers or suppliers

(A) Temporary moratorium imposed by the Secretary

(i) In general

Subject to clause (ii), the State complies with any temporary moratorium on the enrollment of new providers or suppliers imposed by the Secretary under section 1395cc(j)(7) of this title.

(ii) Exceptions

(I) Compliance with moratorium

A State shall not be required to comply with a temporary moratorium described in clause (i) if the State determines that the imposition of such temporary moratorium would adversely impact beneficiaries' access to medical assistance.

(II) FFP available

Notwithstanding section 1396b(i)(2)(E) of this title, payment may be made to a State under this subchapter with respect to amounts expended for items and services described in such section if the Secretary, in consultation with the State agency administering the State plan under this subchapter (or a waiver of the plan), determines that denying payment to the State pursuant to such section would adversely impact beneficiaries' access to medical assistance.

(iii) Limitation on charges to beneficiaries

With respect to any amount expended for items or services furnished during calendar quarters beginning on or after October 1, 2017, the State prohibits, during the period of a temporary moratorium described in clause (i), a provider meeting the requirements specified in subparagraph (C)(iii) of section 1395cc(j)(7) of this title from charging an individual or other person eligible to receive medical assistance under the State plan under this subchapter (or a waiver of the plan) for an item or service described in section 1396b(i)(2)(E) of this title furnished to such an individual.

(B) Moratorium on enrollment of providers and suppliers

At the option of the State, the State imposes, for purposes of entering into participation agreements with providers or suppliers under the State plan or under a waiver of the plan, periods of enrollment moratoria, or numerical caps or other limits, for providers or suppliers identified by the Secretary as being at high-risk for fraud, waste, or abuse as necessary to combat fraud, waste, or abuse, but only if the State determines that the imposition of any such period, cap, or other limits would not adversely impact beneficiaries' access to medical assistance.

(5) Compliance programs

The State requires providers and suppliers under the State plan or under a waiver of the plan to establish, in accordance with the requirements of section 1395cc(j)(7) 1 of this title, a compliance program that contains the core elements established under subparagraph (B) of that section 1395cc(j)(7) 1 of this title for providers or suppliers within a particular industry or category.

(6) Reporting of adverse provider actions

The State complies with the national system for reporting criminal and civil convictions, sanctions, negative licensure actions, and other adverse provider actions to the Secretary, through the Administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, in accordance with regulations of the Secretary.

(7) Enrollment and NPI of ordering or referring providers

The State requires—

(A) all ordering or referring physicians or other professionals to be enrolled under the State plan or under a waiver of the plan as a participating provider; and

(B) the national provider identifier of any ordering or referring physician or other professional to be specified on any claim for payment that is based on an order or referral of the physician or other professional.

(8) Provider terminations

(A) In general

Beginning on July 1, 2018, in the case of a notification under subsection (a)(41) with respect to a termination for a reason specified in section 455.101 of title 42, Code of Federal Regulations (as in effect on November 1, 2015) or for any other reason specified by the Secretary, of the participation of a provider of services or any other person under the State plan (or under a waiver of the plan), the State, not later than 30 days after the effective date of such termination, submits to the Secretary with respect to any such provider or person, as appropriate—

(a) The State Medicaid agency must require all enrolled providers to be screened under to this subpart.

(c) The State Medicaid agency may rely on the results of the provider screening performed by any of the following:

cd8bd8eff7b8ad3f.text:
[getSection]
ID: sec:doc:federal_regulation:42-CFR-455:455.450
Title: Screening levels for Medicaid providers
Section: 455.450
Policy: 42-CFR-455
Type: federal_regulation
Citation link: [42 CFR Part 455](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-455)

Content:
A State Medicaid agency must screen all initial applications, including applications for a new practice location, and any applications received in response to a re-enrollment or revalidation of enrollment request based on a categorical risk level of “limited,” “moderate,” or “high.” If a provider could fit within more than one risk level described in this section, the highest level of screening is applicable.

(a) Screening for providers designated as limited categorical risk. When the State Medicaid agency designates a provider as a limited categorical risk, the State Medicaid agency must do all of the following:

(1) Verify that a provider meets any applicable Federal regulations, or State requirements for the provider type prior to making an enrollment determination.

(2) Conduct license verifications, including State licensure verifications in States other than where the provider is enrolling, in accordance with § 455.412.

(3) Conduct database checks on a pre- and post-enrollment basis to ensure that providers continue to meet the enrollment criteria for their provider type, in accordance with § 455.436.

(b) Screening for providers designated as moderate categorical risk. When the State Medicaid agency designates a provider as a “moderate” categorical risk, a State Medicaid agency must do both of the following:

(1) Perform the “limited” screening requirements described in paragraph (a) of this section.

(2) Conduct on-site visits in accordance with § 455.432.

(c) Screening for providers designated as high categorical risk. When the State Medicaid agency designates a provider as a “high” categorical risk, a State Medicaid agency must do both of the following:

(1) Perform the “limited” and “moderate” screening requirements described in paragraphs (a) and (b) of this section.

(2)(i) Conduct a criminal background check; and

(ii) Require the submission of a set of fingerprints in accordance with § 455.434.

(d) Denial or termination of enrollment. A provider, or any person with 5 percent or greater direct or indirect ownership in the provider, who is required by the State Medicaid agency or CMS to submit a set of fingerprints and fails to do so may have its—

(1) Application denied under § 455.434; or

(2) Enrollment terminated under § 455.416.

(e) Adjustment of risk level. The State agency must adjust the categorical risk level from “limited” or “moderate” to “high” when any of the following occurs:

(1) The State Medicaid agency imposes a payment suspension on a provider based on credible allegation of fraud, waste or abuse, the provider has an existing Medicaid overpayment, or the provider has been excluded by the OIG or another State's Medicaid program within the previous 10 years.

(2) The State Medicaid agency or CMS in the previous 6 months lifted a temporary moratorium for the particular provider type and a provider that was prevented from enrolling based on the moratorium applies for enrollment as a provider at any time within 6 months from the date the moratorium was lifted.

items.question: Who is eligible for the Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)? What requirements does someone have to meet to get in?
items.answer:
## Who can qualify for CAP/DA?

CAP/DA is for adults who need an institutional/nursing-facility level of care but can have their needs met **safely and cost-effectively in the community** with CAP services. It is a Medicaid home- and community-based waiver program under Social Security Act § 1915(c). [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

To enroll, a person generally must:

- Be **age 18 or older** and enrolled in **Medicaid Direct (fee-for-service)**. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- Be approved for **Long-Term Care Medicaid** in one of these categories: Medicaid to the Aged (MAA), Blind (MAB), Disabled (MAD), or Health Care for Workers with Disabilities (HCWD). [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- Meet NC Medicaid’s **home- and community-based-services nursing-facility level of care** because of a documented medical diagnosis or physical disability and functional-care needs. The assessment looks at medical conditions and treatment needs, as well as deficits in activities of daily living (ADLs). [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- Have a completed CAP assessment showing a **reasonable indication of need for at least one CAP/DA waiver service within 30 days** of the evaluation. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- Choose CAP/DA voluntarily, be assigned an available **CAP/DA waiver slot**, and have a signed person-centered service plan authorizing one or more waiver services. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- Be able to live safely in a primary private residence or another approved location with a combination of paid/formal and unpaid/informal supports. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- Have care needs that can be met within the waiver’s average institutional-cost limit, a primary physician who can coordinate medical services, and an emergency backup/disaster plan for times when regular caregivers are unavailable. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## What happens in the application process?

The process begins with a **Service Request Form (SRF)** and physician worksheet to assess clinical eligibility and level of care. The applicant then receives a comprehensive multidisciplinary assessment addressing medical, functional, psychosocial, environmental, financial, and safety-related needs. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

After an approved SRF, the applicant—with assistance from the assessment or case-management entity—starts the application for the required Long-Term Care Medicaid determination. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Is there a waiting list?

Yes. CAP/DA generally considers people first-come, first-served because waiver slots are limited. Certain people receive priority on an existing waitlist, including people transitioning from CAP/C between ages 18 and 20, some nursing-facility transitions, people at risk of abuse/neglect/exploitation with APS protection orders, people with Alzheimer’s disease or a related disorder, certain people transitioning from another NC 1915(c) waiver, and hospice recipients at risk of institutional placement. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

The current Policy 3K-2 was amended September 1, 2025, to implement the CMS-approved CAP/DA waiver renewal effective November 1, 2024. [Policy 3K-2 Revision — 2025-09-01 (All sections and attachments)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

---

items.question: Under the Orthotics and Prosthetics policy, which DME items does NC Medicaid exclude from coverage, and what conditions have to be satisfied for an item to be covered at all?
items.answer:
## Coverage standard

NC Medicaid covers orthotic and prosthetic devices only when the beneficiary’s treating physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner prescribes the item **and** medical necessity is documented. The policy defines medical necessity here as an item needed to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level. [Policy 5B § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

An item is also not covered if the beneficiary does not meet Policy 5B’s eligibility or service criteria, if it duplicates another provider’s item or service, or if it is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial. [Policy 5B § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

Items not listed in Policy 5B’s Attachment B or its fee schedule may still be considered through prior-authorization review for medical necessity when requested by a provider, or by a beneficiary through a provider. [Policy 5B § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Specifically excluded devices and supplies

Policy 5B excludes:

- Devices intended for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience, or for a caregiver’s convenience. [Policy 5B § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)
- Backup devices and duplicates kept at different locations. [Policy 5B § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)
- Devices and supplies for nursing-facility residents. [Policy 5B § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)
- Devices or supplies that another agency covers. [Policy 5B § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)
- Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care, subject to the policy’s care-coordination provision. [Policy 5B § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

## Beneficiaries under 21

For a beneficiary under 21, EPSDT can permit policy limits or specific coverage criteria to be exceeded or not applied when provider documentation establishes that the requested item is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate the child’s condition. EPSDT does not require coverage of an item that is unsafe, ineffective, experimental or investigational, nonmedical, or not generally accepted medical practice. [Policy 5B § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

items.question: For outpatient behavioral health under NC Medicaid: what must be true for someone to start services, to keep receiving them, and to be discharged from them?
items.answer:
NC Medicaid’s current outpatient behavioral-health policy requires **admission criteria to be met to start**, a **two-part showing to continue**, and **one listed ground for discharge**. The policy is current as amended April 15, 2025. [Policy 8C Change Notice 2025-04-15](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## To start outpatient services

The service must be medically necessary, individualized and consistent with the person’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis, safely furnished, not exceed the person’s needs, and not be primarily for convenience; there also cannot be an equally effective, more conservative, or less costly statewide alternative. [Policy 8C § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

For admission, **all** of these must be true:

- The person has a current DSM-5 (or later edition) diagnosis. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)
- They have behavioral, psychological, or biological dysfunction and functional impairment that is consistent with and associated with that diagnosis. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)
- They can develop symptom-management skills, make behavioral changes, and respond favorably to therapy. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)
- There is no evidence that another intervention would be more effective under NC community-practice standards. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

Even where a higher level of care is clinically indicated, outpatient services may be provided while that care is unavailable or when the person refuses it, including to support engagement in the higher level of care. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

### Required beginning documentation

Before outpatient individual, family, or group therapy, a licensed professional must complete a comprehensive clinical assessment (CCA) demonstrating medical necessity; the clinician may update a recent substantially equivalent assessment that reflects the person’s current functioning. [Policy 8C § 7.3.3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

A person-centered treatment/service plan must be completed within 15 business days after the first face-to-face contact, based on the assessment and developed with the beneficiary or legally responsible person. It must identify expected outcomes, strategies, responsible staff, a review schedule, and a way to assess outcomes. [Policy 8C § 7.3.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## To keep receiving services

The beneficiary must satisfy **both** parts of the continued-service test:

1. **At least one ongoing clinical-need factor:** the planned outcome or functioning has not been restored, improved, or sustained in the treatment-plan timeframe; **or** the person remains at risk of relapse based on current assessment and history; **or** functional gains remain tenuous. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

2. **Plus at least one reason further treatment is warranted:** the person achieved current goals but documented symptoms show additional goals are needed; **or** the person is making satisfactory progress and documentation supports that continued service is expected to address the plan’s goals effectively. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

For documentation, every treatment encounter needs a progress note tying the contact and interventions to plan goals, describing response/effectiveness or progress, duration, and clinician signature/credentials. The notes collectively must meaningfully show the person’s response to treatment over time. [Policy 8C § 7.3.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

The plan must be reviewed as needed and at least annually, and a new plan is required at least annually. [Policy 8C § 7.3.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

NC Medicaid does **not** require prior approval for outpatient behavioral-health services. [Policy 8C § 5.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

## To be discharged

Only **one** of these discharge criteria must be met:

- The person’s functioning has improved in relation to the goals in the treatment plan; **or** [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)
- The beneficiary, or legally responsible person, no longer wants the services; **or** [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)
- Despite treatment-plan modifications, the person has not improved and, based on their presentation, needs a more appropriate best-practice or evidence-based treatment modality. [Policy 8C § 3.2.1.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8c-outpatient-behavioral-health-services-provided-direct-enrolled-providers/download?attachment)

items.question: For a child under 21 receiving outpatient therapy, how does the EPSDT provision change what's covered, and who is permitted to order the therapy?
items.answer:
For a Medicaid beneficiary **under age 21**, EPSDT can expand outpatient therapy coverage beyond the ordinary limits in Policy 10A. A limitation on the service’s scope, amount, duration, frequency, location, or other policy criterion may be exceeded—or may not apply—when documentation establishes that the therapy is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate the child’s condition, including to improve or maintain health, compensate for the problem, prevent worsening, or prevent additional problems. EPSDT does not require coverage of services that are unsafe, ineffective, experimental/investigational, nonmedical, or not generally accepted medical treatment. [Policy 10A § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

That does **not** eliminate prior authorization. The policy requires prior approval before treatment begins for beneficiaries under 21, and the provider must submit material showing that the EPSDT criteria are met (and evidence-based literature if available). For LEA-provided therapy, the prior-approval requirement is deemed met through an IEP, IFSP, IHP, BIP, or Section 504 plan process. [Policy 10A § 5.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) Outpatient speech-language therapy specifically remains covered when medically necessary and prior authorization is received. [Policy 10A § 3.2.1.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

**Who may order the outpatient specialized therapy:** the order must come from an **NC Medicaid-enrolled** MD, DO, DPM, certified nurse midwife, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner. [Policy 10A § 3.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

Policy 10A is currently effective **February 1, 2025**. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

items.question: My mother lives in an adult care home (assisted living). Can she receive Personal Care Services through NC Medicaid while living there?
items.answer:
**Yes—potentially.** NC Medicaid covers Personal Care Services (PCS) for a beneficiary who lives in a North Carolina–licensed Adult Care Home (assisted living) if she meets the program’s functional and medical criteria. She must have unmet needs involving either three qualifying activities of daily living (ADLs) with limited hands-on help, two ADLs with one requiring extensive help, or two ADLs with one requiring full-dependence assistance. [Policy 3L-1 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

She must also meet other conditions, including that the home is safe and appropriately inspected, no other payer is responsible for the PCS, the needed services are tied to her documented condition or impairment, she is under a physician’s ongoing direct care for that condition, and she is medically stable rather than needing continuous licensed-nurse care or monitoring. [Policy 3L-1 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

Covered PCS can include hands-on ADL help, related cueing or prompting, certain medication assistance, help with assistive devices or durable medical equipment, and specified Nurse Aide II/delegated monitoring tasks. [Policy 3L-1 § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

However, PCS does **not** pay the assisted-living home’s room and board, and it does not cover transportation, errands, companion sitting, routine ongoing supervision, or skilled nursing provided by an RN or LPN. [Policy 3L-1 § 4.2.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

The current Policy 3L-1 document is marked as amended January 1, 2026. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

judge.explanation: The agent's answer is highly accurate and complete. It correctly identifies Policy 3L-1 as the governing policy for PCS in congregate settings (Adult Care Homes), accurately describes the ADL criteria from Section 3.2.1, lists the additional eligibility conditions, describes covered services from Section 3.3, and correctly notes exclusions from Section 4.2.1.2 including room and board. All claims are supported by the Evidence block. The amendment date of January 1, 2026 is confirmed in the evidence. Citations are precise and section-level. A Medicaid policy expert would find this answer thorough and accurate.

items.question: I want to see a chiropractor — is that something Clinical Coverage Policy 5B pays for?
items.answer:
**No.** Clinical Coverage Policy 5B does not pay for a visit to a chiropractor; it governs coverage of **orthotic and prosthetic devices and related services**, not chiropractic treatment. It covers those devices only when the beneficiary meets its ordering, medical-necessity, encounter, and device-specific requirements. [Policy 5B § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

If you are **under 21**, EPSDT can require coverage of medically necessary services that correct or ameliorate a health problem, subject to the limits described in that provision; Policy 5B itself does not establish chiropractic-visit coverage. [Policy 5B § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

If you tell me whether you have NC Medicaid Direct or a managed-care plan, I can check the policy that may govern chiropractic or similar back-pain treatment.

items.question: A CAP/DA participant wants to switch to a different service provider. Is that allowed, and what rules apply when an eligible beneficiary transfers?
items.answer:
**Yes.** A CAP/DA participant may change to another willing, qualified service provider. CAP/DA’s free-choice provision allows a Medicaid-eligible beneficiary to seek care from any willing and qualified provider, and a provider-agency change requires the beneficiary (or responsible party) to sign a freedom-of-choice form.

## Change of provider agency

The CME must make a plan-of-care (POC) update for the provider-agency change; the policy specifically says that this change is not considered a POC revision.

The broader POC rule also says that changes in a service provider trigger CME responsibility to revise the POC when the beneficiary’s needs change, and the beneficiary or primary caregiver generally must agree to, sign, and date the service plan acknowledging CAP/DA changes.

## Transfer to another county or CME

When an eligible beneficiary asks to transfer to another county or entity, the CME must coordinate the transfer by the agreed transition date or within 30 calendar days or less after the request.

Before transfer, the CME must coordinate the anticipated service start date, transition planning between provider agencies, health/safety/well-being planning, transfer of the electronic record in the CAP Business System, and services starting on the first transfer date.

The receiving entity must arrange a home visit within five business days after the person moves to the new primary residence, to assess the setting and identify and address health-and-welfare concerns.

An active participant who was already approved for CAP/DA may continue participating after moving counties and remains CAP/DA-eligible regardless of county of residence; ongoing Medicaid eligibility is addressed at the next Medicaid certification period.

If the receiving county has a CAP/DA waitlist, the transferring participant is in a priority category and is guaranteed an immediate slot in that county.

## Current policy version

These rules are in the current Policy 3K-2 effective September 1, 2025; the accompanying revision notice states that the policy was updated to align with the CMS-approved CAP/DA waiver renewal.

items.question: For Health Coverage for Workers with Disabilities: is there a ceiling on how much a person can earn from work and still qualify, and do enrollees have to pay premiums?
items.answer:
**There is not a stated ceiling on earnings from work in the HCWD rule.** Instead, the policy says a person is ineligible if their **unearned** income exceeds **150% of the federal poverty level (FPL)**; it treats higher *countable* income as a cost-sharing issue rather than an eligibility cutoff. Work-related exclusions must be applied when countable income is determined. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)

**Yes, some enrollees must pay charges:**

- At or below **150% FPL** in total countable income: no cost sharing other than applicable copayments. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)
- Above **150% FPL**: a **$50 enrollment fee** for each 12-month certification period. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)
- Above **200% FPL** in monthly countable income: a **monthly premium** is also due, in addition to the enrollment fee. The premium rises with income; above **450% FPL**, the person pays the full premium. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)
- Members of federally recognized Native American tribes and Alaska Natives are exempt from cost sharing, including enrollment fees and premiums. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)

The latest amendment located updated the HCWD premium-income chart, with the 2025 FPL changes effective **April 1, 2025**. The current dollar amounts for the monthly premium tiers were not reproduced in the policy text surfaced here. [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 03-25, 2025 Federal Poverty Level Changes (FPL) Income Changes](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/CN-NO-03-25.docx.pdf)

---

items.question: Which federal statute lets North Carolina operate the CAP/DA waiver, and what does the state have to demonstrate to CMS in its waiver application?
items.answer:
North Carolina operates CAP/DA under [SSA § 1915(c)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19), the Medicaid home- and community-based services (HCBS) waiver authority. It permits the Secretary to approve Medicaid payment for HCBS under a written plan of care when, without those services, a person would require hospital, nursing-facility, or ICF/IID-level care. [SSA § 1915(c)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)

What North Carolina must show CMS

Statutory assurances: the State must give satisfactory assurances that it will protect participants’ health and welfare, maintain adequate provider-participation standards, and ensure financial accountability; evaluate potentially eligible people’s need for institutional level of care; inform people likely to need institutional care about feasible waiver alternatives and permit their choice among them; show that estimated average per-person waiver spending will not exceed what the State reasonably estimates it would have spent for those people without the waiver; and report annual information, under the Secretary’s data-collection plan, about the waiver’s effect on Medicaid assistance and participants’ health and welfare. [SSA § 1915(c)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)

The implementing regulation requires the waiver request to include the assurances and supporting documentation, any requested waivers of statewideness, comparability, or applicable medically-needy community income/resource rules, and a statement about whether the agency will refuse HCBS when cost would exceed equivalent care in a hospital, NF, or ICF/IID. [42 CFR § 441.301](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

For an HCBS waiver, the request must provide that services are furnished under a written person-centered service plan approved by the Medicaid agency; only to beneficiaries who are not inpatients of a hospital, NF, or ICF/IID; and only to beneficiaries who would, without the services, require the Medicaid covered level of care in a hospital, NF, or ICF/IID. [42 CFR § 441.301](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) It must also describe the qualifications of the plan developer, the group served, the services to be furnished, and the documentation requirements regarding individual evaluation. [42 CFR § 441.301](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

The application must further include a person-centered planning process led by the individual or authorized representative, with informed choice, accessible information, conflict-resolution procedures, and protections against case-management/provider conflicts of interest; the written plan must be based on assessed functional need and individual preferences. [42 CFR § 441.301](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

North Carolina’s CAP/DA policy also implements these concepts by requiring an HCBS nursing-facility level-of-care determination, documented medical diagnosis and functional need, a CAP assessment showing reasonably indicated need for a CAP/DA service plan, an authorized service plan intended to mitigate institutionalization, ability to remain safe in the community with supports, and paid care maintained within the waiver’s average institutional cost. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

The current CAP/DA policy revision became effective September 1, 2025, and reports that CMS approved the CAP/DA renewal waiver effective November 1, 2024. [Policy 3K-2 Change Notice 2025-09-01](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

judge.explanation: The agent's answer correctly identifies SSA § 1915(c) as the authorizing statute, accurately describes all the statutory assurances NC must provide (health/welfare safeguards, financial accountability, LOC evaluation, informed choice of alternatives, cost-neutrality, annual reporting), and correctly cites 42 CFR § 441.301 and § 441.303 for the regulatory requirements. The answer also correctly references NC Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2 with specific section citations. All claims are supported by the Evidence block - the statutory text of § 1915(c)(2)(A)-(E) is fully reproduced, the CFR sections are present, and Policy 3K-2 § 3.2.1 is referenced. The agent goes beyond the reference answer in useful ways (person-centered planning requirements, HCBS settings requirements) that are all supported by the evidence. No major hallucinations are present. Citation quality is excellent with specific section-level references throughout.

items.question: How many days of therapeutic leave per year can a nursing facility resident take under NC Medicaid, and what conditions apply to that leave?
items.answer:
A Medicaid-eligible nursing facility resident may take **up to 60 days of therapeutic leave in a calendar year** while Medicaid continues paying for the reserved nursing-facility bed. The resident must be occupying a bed for which Medicaid is paying at the time leave begins. [Policy 2B-1 § 5.8](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)

**Conditions for the leave:**

- The leave must be **for therapeutic purposes only**, ordered by the resident’s attending physician, included as necessary in the resident’s plan of care, and supported by a therapeutic justification entered in the health record for **each** leave instance. [Policy 2B-1 § 5.8](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)
- The facility must reserve the resident’s bed and may receive only the Medicaid bed reimbursement during the absence; it is paid the full current Medicaid bed rate for approved therapeutic-leave days. [Policy 2B-1 § 5.8](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)
- A resident may not take **more than 15 consecutive therapeutic-leave days** without NC Medicaid approval. The facility must request prior approval for a longer consecutive leave through the DHHS utilization-review contractor. [Policy 2B-1 § 5.8](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)
- Medicaid does not pay therapeutic-leave days above the legal limit, and the facility must keep cumulative leave records and list residents on leave on its midnight census. [Policy 2B-1 § 5.8](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)
- Therapeutic leave does **not** apply when the resident leaves to receive Medicaid-paid inpatient or nursing services elsewhere, or at a different level of care in the same facility. Ambulance transportation to a therapeutic-leave location is not treated as an emergency and is not Medicaid-reimbursable. [Policy 2B-1 § 5.8](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)

The current Policy 2B-1 was posted August 7, 2024, with an amended date of August 1, 2024; the revision notice identifies an update to § 5.8. [Policy 2B-1 Change Notice 2024-08-01](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment)

items.question: What notice is a Private Duty Nursing provider required to give before it stops serving a Medicaid beneficiary?
items.answer:
A PDN provider that discharges a beneficiary must notify **NC Medicaid—not the beneficiary—within five business days** of the discharge.  

- **For beneficiaries age 21 or older:** the provider must submit the **DMA-3513 PDN Discharge Summary Form** within five business days. If the discharge is because another source will cover nursing care, the notice must give the last Medicaid-billable service date and identify the other coverage source. [Policy 3G-1 § 5.2.4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)  
- **For beneficiaries under 21:** the provider must send NC Medicaid a copy of the **physician’s order terminating services** within five business days. If another coverage source is taking over, the provider must notify NC Medicaid in writing, stating the last Medicaid-billable PDN date and the other coverage source. [Policy 3G-2 § 5.2.4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-2-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-under-21-years-age/download?attachment)  

The cited PDN policies do **not** state a particular advance-notice period that the provider must give the beneficiary before ending services. [Policy 3G-1 § 5.2.4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment) [Policy 3G-2 § 5.2.4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-2-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-under-21-years-age/download?attachment)

judge.explanation: The agent's answer is accurate and well-supported by the evidence. It correctly identifies the five-business-day notification requirement to NC Medicaid, the DMA-3513 form for beneficiaries 21+, and the physician's order requirement for beneficiaries under 21. It also correctly notes the additional requirements when another coverage source exists. The agent appropriately distinguishes between the two policies (3G-1 and 3G-2) and honestly notes that neither policy specifies an advance notice period to the beneficiary. All claims are supported by the evidence blocks. Citations are precise, referencing specific section numbers (5.2.4.1) and policy numbers (3G-1, 3G-2) with URLs.

items.question: I was approved for Personal Care Services but got fewer than 80 hours a month. How long do I have to wait before I can ask for a reconsideration to get more hours?
items.answer:
Assuming your approval is under the congregate-settings PCS program, yes—if you are **18 or older** and this was your **initial PCS approval for fewer than 80 hours per month**, you must wait **30 calendar days after the date on the approval notification**. You may file the reconsideration request starting on **day 31**, and it must be filed **no later than day 60** after that notification. [Policy 3L-1 § 5.6](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

You need to submit **NC Medicaid Form 3114** to the Comprehensive Independent Assessment Entity (CIAE), with documents explaining why you need more hours and which daily-living tasks are not being met with the hours currently approved. [Policy 3L-1 § 5.6](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

**Important exception:** If your condition or needs have changed and you meet the change-of-status criteria, you can request a **Change of Status review at any time**—the 30-day wait does not apply. [Policy 3L-1 § 5.6](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

items.question: Under federal Medicaid law, what counts as 'home health services' and in what setting must they be furnished?
items.answer:
Under federal **Medicaid** rules, “home health services” are covered services provided to a beneficiary **at the beneficiary’s place of residence** and under the required written practitioner orders and plan of care. [42 CFR § 440.70 (last revised 2020-05-08)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

They include:

- **Part-time or intermittent nursing services;**
- **Home health aide services;**
- **Medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** suitable for settings where normal life activities occur; and
- At the state’s option, **physical therapy, occupational therapy, and speech pathology/audiology services.** [42 CFR § 440.70 (last revised 2020-05-08)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

The first three categories are required home-health benefits, and a state may not make coverage conditional on the person also needing nursing or therapy. [42 CFR § 440.70 (last revised 2020-05-08)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Required setting

“Place of residence” is broad: the regulation permits home-health services in **any setting where normal life activities take place.** The beneficiary does **not** have to be homebound. [42 CFR § 440.70 (last revised 2020-05-08)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

But it generally does **not** include a **hospital, nursing facility, intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID), or another setting where Medicaid pays or could pay for inpatient services that include room and board.** There is a narrow ICF/IID exception for home-health services that the facility itself is not required to provide—for example, short-term RN care during an acute illness to prevent transfer to a nursing facility. [42 CFR § 440.70 (last revised 2020-05-08)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Ordering requirement

For nursing, aide, and therapy services, the order may be written by a physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant acting under state law, as part of a written plan of care reviewed by the ordering practitioner every 60 days. [42 CFR § 440.70 (last revised 2020-05-08)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

---

- [42 CFR § 440.70(b)(3)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

It correctly identifies all components of home health services under 42 CFR § 440.70: required services (nursing, home health aide, medical supplies/equipment/appliances) and optional services (PT, OT, speech pathology/audiology). It accurately describes the setting requirement ('place of residence' broadly defined, excluding hospitals, nursing facilities, ICF/IID except for narrow exception), the ordering requirements (physician, NP, CNS, or PA per state law, written plan of care reviewed every 60 days), the prohibition on homebound requirement, and the face-to-face encounter requirement. items.question: To elect hospice under NC Medicaid, what does it mean to be 'terminally ill', and who has to certify that prognosis?
items.answer:
To be **“terminally ill”** for NC Medicaid hospice, the beneficiary must have a medical prognosis that—if the illness follows its normal course—life expectancy is **six months or less**. [Policy 3D § 1.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)

For the **initial 90-day hospice benefit period**, the hospice must obtain written certification from **(1) the hospice medical director or a physician member of the hospice interdisciplinary group, and (2) the beneficiary’s attending physician, if the beneficiary has one**. [Policy 3D § 5.4.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) For later benefit periods, certification by the **hospice medical director or physician member of the interdisciplinary group** alone is required. [Policy 3D § 5.4.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)

The certification must be written, signed and dated by the certifying physician, and include the applicable benefit-period dates. [Policy 3D § 5.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) It also must include a brief physician narrative explaining the clinical basis for the terminal prognosis, tailored to the person’s individual clinical circumstances. [Policy 3D Attachment B, Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)

NC Medicaid’s current Policy 3D is effective March 15, 2024; its March 2024 revision concerned an Attachment A billing value code, not these terminal-illness certification rules. [Policy 3D Change Notice 2024-03-15](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment)

judge.explanation: The agent's answer is fully accurate and complete. It correctly defines 'terminally ill' as a prognosis of 6 months or less if the illness runs its normal course (per §1.1.4), correctly identifies the dual certification requirement for the initial 90-day period (hospice medical director/IDG physician + attending physician if one exists) per §5.4.3, and correctly notes that subsequent periods require only the hospice medical director/IDG physician. The agent goes beyond the reference answer to add accurate details about written certification requirements, the physician narrative requirement (from Attachment D/§_s129), and the 2024 amendment note — all of which are supported by the Evidence block. No hallucinations are present; all claims trace back to evidence. Citations are precise and section-level (1.1.4, 5.4.3, 5.4, Attachment B).

items.question: When will NC Medicaid refuse to pay for an ambulance trip — which ambulance transports are excluded from coverage?
items.answer:
## When NC Medicaid can refuse ambulance payment

NC Medicaid will not pay an ambulance claim when the beneficiary is not eligible for the service, the trip fails the policy’s coverage criteria, it duplicates another provider’s service, or it is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial. Ambulance transportation also must be medically necessary—not primarily for the convenience of the patient, caregiver, or provider—and there cannot be an equally effective, more conservative, or less costly option available statewide. [Policy 15 § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment) [Policy 15 § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

More specifically, the policy excludes or does not reimburse:

- **A trip to a destination outside the covered destination list.** Covered destinations are limited to listed facilities and locations, including hospitals, skilled-nursing facilities, adult care homes, ICF-IIDs, the person’s primary residence, qualifying dialysis facilities, airport/helipad transfer sites, and certain physician-office trips. [Policy 15 § 3.2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- **Non-emergency ambulance transportation that is not medically required.** For example, it is covered only where other transportation is medically contraindicated because the person needs stretcher transport, needed care is unavailable where the person lives, or there is a qualifying return transfer to a lower-resource facility. A person who is bed-confined must meet all three conditions: unable to get up without help, unable to walk, and unable to sit in a chair or wheelchair. [Policy 15 § 3.2.2.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- **Travel farther than the nearest appropriate facility.** NC Medicaid does not reimburse loaded mileage to a facility that is not the nearest appropriate one; a patient’s preference or a doctor’s staff privileges does not decide whether a facility is appropriate. [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- **A call where no treatment is needed, a false alarm, or a case where the beneficiary refuses all medical services.** [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- **Transport to receive a service that Medicaid itself does not cover.** [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- **Transport of a person pronounced dead by an authorized individual before the ambulance was called.** [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- **Air-ambulance transport to a non-acute-care hospital.** [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)
- **Separate charges** for commercial airline tickets, airstrip fees, taxes, facility/ambulance-service nursing staff, waiting time, or oxygen and supplies already included in the ambulance base rate. [Policy 15 § 4.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

For an unscheduled or non-repetitive non-emergency trip involving someone under a physician’s care, the provider generally needs a written medical-necessity order within 48 hours; a signature from specified clinical personnel may substitute in defined circumstances. But paperwork alone does not establish coverage—the provider still must show medical necessity and satisfy all coverage and call-report requirements. [Policy 15 § 7.3.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

For a beneficiary **under 21**, EPSDT can permit policy limits to be exceeded or not applied when documentation establishes that the service is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate a health condition; EPSDT does not require coverage of care that is unsafe, ineffective, experimental/investigational, nonmedical, or not generally accepted medical practice. [Policy 15 § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

---

*Suggested citations for uncited claims above:*
- [Policy 15 § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment)

items.question: Does NC Medicaid limit the quantity of a prescription that can be dispensed, and in what situations does a pharmacy claim need prior authorization?
items.answer:
**Yes.** Under NC Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy 9, the usual maximum dispensing amount is a **34-day supply** for any drug, unless an exception applies. The current version was amended effective July 15, 2024. [Policy 9 § 5.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

Key exceptions include:

- Up to **12 months of oral birth-control medication** and up to **three months of prepackaged hormone-replacement therapy** may be dispensed. [Policy 9 § 5.4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)
- A prescriber may authorize a **90-day supply** of a **non-controlled maintenance medication**. [Policy 9 § 5.4.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)
- NC Medicaid may set drug-specific quantity limits for **episodic drugs**—medicines intended for intermittent rather than daily use—using FDA labeling, evidence-based guidance, and recommendations of the North Carolina Physician Advisory Group. The applicable limit is in the Preferred Drug List or the drug’s specific prior-authorization policy. [Policy 9 § 5.4.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)
- For a beneficiary under age 21, ordinary amount, duration, and frequency limits may be exceeded when provider documentation establishes that the product is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate the child’s condition under EPSDT. [Policy 9 § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

## When prior authorization is needed

A pharmacy claim needs PA when the prescribed drug is among NC Medicaid’s **selected PA drugs**. Attachment K identifies drug categories and products requiring PA, including, for example, GLP-1 receptor agonists and combinations, hepatitis C medications, growth hormones, opioid analgesics, PCSK9 inhibitors, continuous glucose-monitoring systems and supplies, and certain behavioral-health clinical edits. Each listed drug has its own medical-necessity criteria. [Policy 9 Attachment K](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

PA may also be required for a **new-to-market product** or an existing product with a new variation, indication, indication change, or dosing change while NC Medicaid conducts its clinical review and has not yet adopted—or decided it does not need—specific coverage criteria. During that interim period, coverage is based on FDA indications, FDA-approved doses, and medically accepted indications, and may involve PA for both fee-for-service Medicaid and Medicaid managed-care plans. [Policy 9 § 5.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment) [Policy 9 Change Notice 3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

Finally, if the requested **indication or dose falls outside FDA-approved guidance, evidence-based standards, or NC Medicaid drug criteria**, the prescriber may request approval based on medical necessity. The request must include medical-record support, an explanation of prior drug trials or why they cannot be tried, the prescriber’s explanation for why ordinary criteria are inadequate, and supporting compendia or peer-reviewed literature. [Policy 9 § 3.2.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

---

- [Policy 9 § 5.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

items.question: Can my daughter receive her speech therapy sessions over video? What does NC Medicaid require before speech therapy can be delivered via telehealth?
items.answer:
## Yes—some speech-language services can be provided by video.

NC Medicaid permits a select set of speech and language evaluation and treatment services through telehealth, subject to the telehealth requirements and the billable-code list in Clinical Coverage Policy 10A. [Policy 10A § 3.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

Before telehealth speech therapy is used, the provider must determine that it is medically necessary or appropriate for **your daughter**, such as when her medical condition means she should avoid exposure to others, or when she lives in a remote or underserved area with limited access to qualified providers. [Policy 10A § e. Telehealth](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

The key conditions are:

- **Video therapy generally must supplement, not replace, in-person care.** It may replace in-person care only when in-person treatment is contraindicated or unavailable. [Policy 10A § e. Telehealth](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
- **It must be in your daughter’s best interest**, not simply more convenient for the therapist. [Policy 10A § e. Telehealth](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
- **It cannot be used solely to increase a therapist’s productivity.** [Policy 10A § e. Telehealth](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
- The usual speech-language therapy rules still apply: the therapy must be medically necessary and must receive prior authorization. [Policy 10A § 3.2.1.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
- The authorized number of visits must be medically necessary based on the severity of the deficit, and an authorization period cannot exceed six calendar months. [Policy 10A § 5.4.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

The current Policy 10A cited here is effective February 1, 2025. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)
