items.question: Federal law sets a minimum medical loss ratio for Medicaid managed care plans — what is that requirement, and how has North Carolina implemented it?
items.answer:
## Federal requirement

Federal law has **two distinct MLR rules**:

1. **Rate-setting benchmark:** CMS may approve Medicaid managed-care capitation rates only if they are developed so the MCO, PIHP, or PAHP would *reasonably achieve* an MLR of **at least 85%** for the rate year. The rates may target a higher MLR if they still cover reasonable, appropriate, and attainable non-benefit costs. [42 CFR § 438.4(b)(9) (last revised 2020-11-13)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

2. **Plan-level reporting and a conditional state minimum:** States must contractually require plans to calculate and report MLRs under the federal methodology. But the regulation does **not** independently require every state to impose a retrospective 85% plan-level minimum: **if a state elects** to impose one, its minimum must be at least 85%. [42 CFR § 438.8(a), (c) (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

The federal MLR is the ratio of specified spending—principally incurred claims, quality-improvement activities, and fraud-prevention activities—to the defined revenue denominator, subject to the regulation’s inclusions, exclusions, and possible credibility adjustment. [42 CFR § 438.8(d)–(e) (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

Federal oversight also requires the state to annually submit to CMS, with its rate certification, a plan-by-plan summary that includes the MLR numerator, denominator, achieved percentage, member months, and any remittances owed. [42 CFR § 438.74(a) (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438) If a state contract requires remittances for failing its state minimum, the state must repay CMS the federal share and report the method used to allocate the state and federal shares. [42 CFR § 438.74(b) (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

The most recent Federal Register amendment shown for § 438.74 is **89 FR 41276 (May 10, 2024)**; for § 438.8, it is **89 FR 41272 (May 10, 2024)**. [42 CFR § 438.74 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438) [42 CFR § 438.8 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## North Carolina’s implementation

North Carolina went beyond the federal prospective 85% rate-setting benchmark by establishing a **statewide 88% minimum MLR threshold for health-care services** in Medicaid Transformation. [NC PHP Contract § 15.4.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

NC DHHS requires each prepaid health plan (PHP) to calculate and report aggregate MLR annually and retrospectively on both a **CMS-defined** formula and a **DHHS-defined** formula. [NC PHP Contract § 15.4.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

For the DHHS-defined measure, the individual PHP’s minimum is based on its actual capitation-revenue mix across specified rating groups, using a revenue-weighted average of DHHS-defined factors calibrated to the 88% threshold. [NC PHP Contract § 15.4.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

If a PHP’s DHHS-defined MLR falls below its applicable minimum, it must remit a rebate to DHHS equal to the DHHS-defined denominator multiplied by the gap between the minimum threshold and the PHP’s result; qualifying contributions to health-related resources may substitute for some or all of that rebate. [NC PHP Contract § 15.4.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

In short: **85% is the federal actuarial-soundness benchmark and the floor for any state-chosen retrospective minimum; North Carolina chose an 88% retrospective DHHS-defined threshold with an annual reporting-and-remittance mechanism.** [42 CFR § 438.4(b)(9) (last revised 2020-11-13)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438) [42 CFR § 438.8(c) (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438) [NC PHP Contract §§ 15.4, 15.4.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/contract-30-190029-dhb-prepaid-health-plan-services-rfp/download?attachment)

judge.explanation: The agent's answer is highly accurate and comprehensive. It correctly identifies the federal MLR framework under 42 CFR 438.8 (requiring states to mandate calculation/reporting, with any state-set minimum at 85% or higher), the rate-setting benchmark under 42 CFR 438.4(b)(9) (85% actuarial soundness), and the state oversight/reporting requirements under 42 CFR 438.74. For North Carolina, it accurately describes the 88% DHHS-defined MLR threshold established under S.L. 2018-49, the dual reporting requirement (CMS-defined and DHHS-defined formulas), the revenue-weighted average methodology across rating groups, and the remittance/rebate mechanism with health-related resource contributions as an alternative. All claims are supported by the evidence blocks. Citations are precise and section-level (42 CFR 438.4(b)(9), 438.8(a)/(c), 438.74, NC PHP Contract 15.4.2). The answer goes beyond the reference answer in useful detail without introducing unsupported claims.

items.question: When does NC Medicaid pay for CAR-T cell treatment? What specific criteria have to be met?
items.answer:
## When NC Medicaid pays for CAR-T therapy

NC Medicaid covers CAR-T cell therapy when it is **medically necessary** and all policy-specific requirements are met. The treatment must be individualized and consistent with the person’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis, safely furnished, not exceed the person’s needs, have no equally effective more conservative or less costly statewide alternative, and not be primarily for convenience. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

The CAR-T product and treatment must also meet **every** one of these conditions:

- The specific CAR-T therapy must be approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- It must be given according to the FDA-approved requirements for its indication and use, dosage and administration, dosage form and strength, and warnings and precautions. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- It must be administered at a certified or authorized treatment center. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- If the product is subject to an FDA Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS), the center must be enrolled in that REMS and its providers must be trained to manage cytokine-release syndrome and neurologic toxicities. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)
- The provider must obtain **prior approval before treatment is provided**. [Policy 11A-17 § 5.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## When it will not be covered

NC Medicaid will not cover CAR-T therapy if the product is not FDA-approved; if it is used outside FDA guidelines for indication/use, administration, or dosage form/strength; or, for a REMS product, if it is given at a facility not enrolled in the required REMS program. [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

It also excludes a repeat CAR-T treatment for someone who previously received another CAR-T therapy, cases where psychosocial history limits the person’s ability to follow required pre- and post-infusion care, and current beneficiary or caretaker noncompliance that makes adherence to the required treatment regimen improbable. [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

A concurrent rescue transplant with CAR-T infusion is excluded as experimental. [Policy 11A-17 § 4.2.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

## Prior-approval submission materials

For prior approval, the treating provider must submit a physician-signed medical-necessity letter describing prior chemotherapy regimens and dates, clinical and social history, and the reasons for CAR-T; proof that the treatment facility is qualified or authorized; HIV and hepatitis serologies generally less than three months old; diagnostic and procedure results including a bone-marrow biopsy generally no more than six months old; and a complete psychological and social evaluation addressing medical compliance, support network, post-treatment plan and care providers, and relevant mental-health, substance-use, or legal history. [Policy 11A-17 § 5.2.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

The cited CAR-T policy is the current version effective **April 1, 2025**. [Policy 11A-17 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment)

items.question: Up to what age can children on Medicaid receive fluoride varnish from their physician, and what oral screening has to accompany it?
items.answer:
Children can receive physician-applied fluoride varnish **from tooth eruption until age 3½**. Medicaid covers up to **six oral-screening packages** during that period. [Policy 1A-23 § 3.2.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

The required accompanying oral screening includes:

- **Early caries screening** and identification of notable findings in the mouth—obvious hard- or soft-tissue pathology—using a **dental mirror and directed light**;
- **Oral-hygiene and nutrition counseling** and educational materials for the child/caregiver;
- A **fluoride supplement prescription when indicated**; and
- Fluoride varnish applied to **all erupted primary teeth**. [Policy 1A-23 § 7.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

The medical record must document the oral evaluation/findings, preventive oral-health and dietary counseling with the primary caregiver, varnish application, and a dental referral when appropriate. [Policy 1A-23 § 7.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

The most recent identified revision, effective April 1, 2023, updated template language rather than these fluoride-service criteria. [Policy 1A-23 Change Notice 2023-04-15](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-23-physician-fluoride-varnish-services/download?attachment)

items.question: An NC Innovations participant's needs cost more than their individual base budget. Can they request services beyond the budget, and what recourse do they have if they think the budget can't meet their needs?
items.answer:
**Yes.** An NC Innovations participant may request services that cost more than the assigned base budget when they believe their needs cannot be met within it. The base budget and SIS results are guidelines—not a binding cap—and medically necessary services must be authorized even if they exceed that budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

The policy also expressly says that a budget increase is **not required** before Utilization Management can approve medically necessary services above the budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

**What to do:**
- Ask the care coordinator and person-centered planning team to include the needed services in an updated Individual Support Plan (ISP) and submit it for Utilization Management review. When a level change produces a budget increase, the policy specifically contemplates an updated ISP being submitted for approval. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)
- If the participant’s needs have changed, an updated Support Intensity Scale (SIS) can lead NC Medicaid or its designee to reassess the person’s level and base budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)
- If the LME/MCO denies a requested service, it must provide the reasons for the decision and instructions on how to appeal. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)
- The participant may also file a **grievance about the base budget** itself. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

One important distinction: the policy describes the individual budget as only one measure of likely needs and says it is reviewed at least annually. It also distinguishes the base-budget amount from the waiver’s overall cost limit, which has separate rules. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

judge.explanation: The agent's answer is factually accurate and complete. It correctly states that the base budget is not a binding cap, that medically necessary services must be authorized regardless of budget, that no budget increase is required before UM can approve services above the budget, and covers all recourse options (updated ISP/SIS, appeal rights on denial, grievance about base budget). All key claims are supported by the evidence blocks. No hallucinations detected — all claims align with the evidence provided.

items.question: What does it take to become a certified HIV case management provider for NC Medicaid, and what circumstances can lead to a provider losing that certification?
items.answer:
## Bottom line

An agency must obtain HIV Case Management certification from NC Medicaid (or its designated contractor) **before it can enroll and be reimbursed as an HIV Case Management provider.** Certification is not permanent: initial certification lasts one year, and recertification generally lasts two years. [Policy 12B § 6.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment) [Policy 12B § 6.2.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment) [Policy 12B § 6.2.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

The current policy reflects the revision posted August 15, 2023, effective April 1, 2023; that revision made template language changes associated with the NC Health Choice transition into Medicaid. [Policy 12B Change Notice 2023-08-15](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

## What it takes to become certified

The provider can be a home health or home care agency, hospice, health department, hospital, DSS, FQHC, rural health clinic, community-based organization, or local management entity—but must meet the certification requirements. [Policy 12B § 6.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

At a high level, the agency must:

- Have a documented successful **three-year record** of providing or managing HIV case-management programs; employ qualified HIV case managers and supervisors; enroll **each physical location** with Medicaid; comply with state and federal provider-participation laws; maintain certification; operate a quality-improvement program; allow record and financial-operational reviews; timely report organizational changes; and achieve national accreditation from an approved accreditor within one year of Medicaid enrollment. [Policy 12B § 6.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- Meet general Medicaid participation requirements, have a current signed DHHS Provider Administrative Participation Agreement, bill only within the provider’s lawful scope of practice, and attest that billed services were medically necessary and actually delivered. [Policy 12B § 6.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- Submit a **complete, signed initial application** with the required administrative, case-management, and human-resources materials; initial certification is valid for one year. [Policy 12B § 6.2.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

### Required operational infrastructure

The application must demonstrate a real operating agency: a non-residential, non-vehicle physical business site verified by site visit; service counties, scheduled hours, an after-hours emergency plan, community-resource list, organizational chart, ownership information, Medicaid-required web-application access, a business plan and financial projections, compliant IT/electronic-record and billing capability, an on-site precertification visit, and applicable licensure/certification. [Policy 12B § 6.2.1—Administrative Requirements](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

It also needs organization-specific written policies addressing confidentiality and informed consent, grievances, beneficiary rights, nondiscrimination, ethics, conflicts of interest, electronic and medical records, freedom of provider choice, transfers/discharges, and abuse/neglect/exploitation. [Policy 12B § 6.2.1—Administrative Requirements](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

The agency must submit a description of how it will provide the core case-management functions and a quality-improvement plan that measures outcomes, audits records, tracks and resolves complaints, examines cost/utilization, assures billing accuracy, and confirms staff qualifications. [Policy 12B § 6.2.1—Case Management Requirements](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

Human-resources requirements include credential-validation, continuing-education, and background-check policies; staffing-contingency and management-delegation plans; supervision, orientation, and annual training plans; and plans to track case-manager competencies. Owners cannot have specified felony convictions involving financial misconduct or beneficiary abuse/neglect in health-care delivery. [Policy 12B § 6.2.1—Human Resource Requirements](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

### Staffing and training

HIV case managers and supervisors must meet the policy’s education, professional-experience, case-management-experience, and HIV-knowledge standards. [Policy 12B § 6.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment) [Policy 12B § 6.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment) [Policy 12B § 6.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

All case managers and supervisors must complete NC state-sponsored basic training within 90 days of employment and before the agency bills for their case-management units; they must also complete 12 annual hours of HIV case-management continuing education, including six clinically oriented hours. [Policy 12B § 6.1.7.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment) [Policy 12B § 6.1.7.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

## Maintaining certification / recertification

For recertification, the provider must return a complete signed application within 60 calendar days of receiving it; provide changed initial-certification materials, staff credentials, annual quality-improvement summaries with outcome metrics, and submit to an on-site record/business review. [Policy 12B § 6.2.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

The recertification checklist specifically asks for staff employment dates, counties and services, operating hours and after-hours coverage, accreditation information, satisfaction-survey practices, and counts of Medicaid and Ryan White clients. [dma-3157 HIV Case Management Provider Recertification Application Checklist](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/dma-3157.pdf) [dma-3158 HIV Case Management Provider Recertification Application](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/dma-3158.pdf)

If an application remains deficient after 90 days, it is returned as incomplete. If a site visit finds noncompliance, NC Medicaid may issue a six-month provisional recertification to allow monitoring and corrective work. [Policy 12B § 6.2.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

## Reasons a provider can lose certification

A provider may be denied certification from the outset if it was previously decertified, its Medicaid provider number is suspended due to Program Integrity sanctions, or it has not repaid money owed to NC Medicaid. [Policy 12B § 6.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

After certification, NC Medicaid or its contractor may decertify—and Medicaid may disenroll—the agency if any listed condition is substantiated. The list is expressly nonexclusive. [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

Important examples include:

- Failing to provide required core case-management services, adequate case-manager supervision, or an effective quality-improvement program. [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- Fraudulent billing, falsified records, documentation that does not support billing, or an owner’s felony conviction. [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- Violating beneficiary confidentiality. [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- Employing staff who do not meet policy qualifications; missing the 90-day basic-training deadline; or failing to obtain required annual continuing education. [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- Not timely submitting required documents, not correcting cited deficiencies through a written correction plan within 30 days, or not reporting agency-name, ownership/director, address, or phone changes within the required time. [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)
- Failing to comply with applicable laws, Medicaid rules, reimbursement requirements, or the certification requirements themselves; or failing to enroll any beneficiaries within four months after certification. [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

Quality-assurance visits can lead to provisional recertification, decertification, or Program Integrity referral when policy violations are found. The agency must submit a requested written corrective-action plan within 30 days, and NC Medicaid may schedule follow-up visits to verify correction. [Policy 12B § 7.8](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

A provider notified that it is no longer certified may seek reconsideration under 10A NCAC 22F.0402. [Policy 12B § 6.2.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/12b-human-immunodeficiency-virus-hiv-case-management/download?attachment)

judge.explanation: The agent's answer is comprehensive and accurate, covering all key aspects of both certification requirements (§6.2.1) and decertification conditions (§6.2.5) as verified against the evidence. The answer correctly identifies: the three-year track record requirement, staffing qualifications, training requirements (90-day basic training, 12 annual CEU hours with 6 clinical), organizational infrastructure requirements, the initial one-year certification period, two-year recertification cycle, and the full list of decertification triggers. All specific claims are supported by the evidence blocks. Citations are precise and section-level throughout (§6.0, §6.1, §6.1.1, §6.1.2, §6.1.4, §6.1.7.1, §6.1.7.2, §6.2.1, §6.2.3, §6.2.4, §6.2.5, §7.8). No hallucinations detected - all facts including the 2023-08-15 amendment reference, the 10A NCAC 22F.0402 reconsideration process, and the provisional six-month recertification provision are supported by the evidence. The answer goes beyond the reference answer in useful detail while remaining accurate.

items.question: Will the Orthotics and Prosthetics policy (5B) pay for chiropractic treatment?
items.answer:
**No.** Clinical Coverage Policy 5B pays for medically necessary **orthotic and prosthetic devices**, not chiropractic treatment. A device must be prescribed by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner and be needed to maintain or improve the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level.

Even an unlisted request under 5B must be for a **device** that meets the definition of an orthotic or prosthetic; that pathway does not turn chiropractic care into a covered 5B service.

For someone under 21, EPSDT can sometimes overcome policy limitations for medically necessary care, but Policy 5B’s EPSDT provision does not make chiropractic treatment an orthotic or prosthetic device covered under this policy.

items.question: If someone wants bariatric or body-contouring surgery purely for cosmetic weight-loss reasons with no medical necessity, does Policy 1A-15 (Surgery for Clinically Severe or Morbid Obesity) cover it?
items.answer:
**No.** Policy 1A-15 covers specified bariatric procedures only when the beneficiary meets the policy’s clinical criteria for clinically severe or morbid obesity, supported by health records; a request based purely on cosmetic weight loss and with no medical necessity would not meet those requirements. [Policy 1A-15 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-15-surgery-clinically-severe-or-morbid-obesity/download?attachment)

For **body-contouring after weight loss**—such as removal of excess skin or fat from the arms, abdomen, or thighs—the policy expressly says surgical removal **solely for cosmetic purposes is not covered**. It directs providers to Policy 1-O-1 for criteria that may apply to excessive-skin removal when it is not solely cosmetic. [Policy 1A-15 § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-15-surgery-clinically-severe-or-morbid-obesity/download?attachment)

Even a bariatric procedure that otherwise could be covered requires the person to satisfy all policy requirements and obtain prior approval when primary insurance does not cover it. [Policy 1A-15 § 5.2.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-15-surgery-clinically-severe-or-morbid-obesity/download?attachment)

The current policy is effective October 1, 2024; its 2024 revisions concerned claims-code tables rather than these coverage standards. [Policy 1A-15 Change Notice 2024-10-01](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1a-15-surgery-clinically-severe-or-morbid-obesity/download?attachment)

items.question: Can an adult over age 21 get routine massage therapy paid for under outpatient therapy Policy 10A?
items.answer:
No. For an adult age 21 or older, Policy 10A covers only medically necessary outpatient specialized therapy services within the listed therapy categories, and massage therapy is not listed as a covered outpatient specialized therapy service in the policy.[Policy 10A § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) [Policy 10A § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

Under Policy 10A, the covered treatment categories are physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech-language therapy, respiratory therapy, and audiology therapy.[Policy 10A § 1.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) The physical therapy coverage section says Medicaid covers medically necessary outpatient physical therapy treatment when prior authorization is received, but it does not identify routine massage therapy as a covered standalone service.[Policy 10A § 3.2.1.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

Policy 10A also says Medicaid does not cover services when the beneficiary does not meet the policy’s Section 3.0 coverage criteria, and it does not cover therapy services that are solely for maintenance.[Policy 10A § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) [Policy 10A § 4.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

For adults 21 and older, even covered therapy treatment requires prior approval and is subject to annual visit limits.[Policy 10A § 5.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

Policy 10A is current effective February 1, 2025, and I did not find any separate change notice amending it in the amendment records returned for this document.[Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment)

items.question: Will the NC Medicaid outpatient pharmacy benefit pay for a drug that is still experimental or investigational?
items.answer:
**No.** NC Medicaid’s outpatient pharmacy benefit does not cover a drug that is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial. The drug also generally must have an FDA-approved indication or a medically accepted indication, unless the Division of Health Benefits approves it. [Policy 9 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment) [Policy 9 § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

For a beneficiary under age 21, EPSDT can override many policy limits when a service is medically necessary—but it **does not** require coverage of a product that is unsafe, ineffective, experimental, or investigational. [Policy 9 § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

This policy was amended effective July 15, 2024; its amendment clarified the FDA-indication/DHB-approval language. [Policy 9 Change Notice 2024-07-15](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

items.question: Under Policy 9 on outpatient pharmacy, are over-the-counter fertility or hormone supplements bought without a prescription covered?
items.answer:
**No.** Policy 9 applies only to *covered* legend drugs and *covered* OTC products dispensed by outpatient pharmacy providers, and it specifically lists both OTC products and fertility drugs as not covered. Thus, an over-the-counter fertility supplement bought without a prescription is not covered; an OTC hormone supplement is likewise not covered as an OTC product. For a beneficiary **under age 21**, Policy 9 directs consideration of the EPSDT exception: limits in a clinical coverage policy may not apply when provider documentation establishes that the requested product is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate a health condition. EPSDT does not require coverage of something unsafe, ineffective, experimental/investigational, nonmedical, or not generally accepted medical treatment. [Policy 9 § 4.0](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment) [Policy 9 § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

items.question: My client's prior authorization request was denied by NC Medicaid. Can we appeal that denial directly to CMS at the federal level?
items.answer:
**No.** A North Carolina Medicaid prior-authorization denial is appealed through the **state Medicaid appeal/fair-hearing process**, not directly to CMS. Federal Medicaid rules specifically require the state agency to offer a hearing for a prior-authorization decision. [42 CFR § 431.220](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-431)

The next step depends on who issued the denial:

- **If NC Medicaid/the state or its contractor issued the PA denial (fee-for-service):** request a **North Carolina State fair hearing**. Federal rules require the state to allow a reasonable filing period, capped at **90 days from the mailing date of the action notice**. An authorized representative may submit the request. [42 CFR § 431.221](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-431)

- **If a Medicaid managed-care plan issued the denial:** the enrollee must first use the plan’s **one internal appeal level**; the plan notice must explain the adverse determination, the right to appeal, and the right to a State fair hearing. The plan-level appeal deadline is **60 calendar days from the date on the denial notice**. [42 CFR § 438.402](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438) After the plan upholds the denial—or if it misses the federal notice/timing requirements—the enrollee may request a **State fair hearing**. [42 CFR § 438.408](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

For a managed-care denial, the appeal decision-makers must have appropriate clinical expertise, and the plan must provide the enrollee or representative the case file, medical records, and evidence used in the decision **free of charge**. [42 CFR § 438.406](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

So, preserve the applicable **plan-appeal or State-fair-hearing deadline shown on the denial notice** rather than sending the merits appeal to CMS.

judge.explanation: The agent's answer correctly states that NC Medicaid PA denials cannot be appealed directly to CMS and must go through the state administrative process. It accurately distinguishes between fee-for-service (state fair hearing, 90-day deadline per 42 CFR §431.221) and managed care (one internal appeal level, 60-day deadline per 42 CFR §438.402, then state fair hearing per 42 CFR §438.408) pathways. All specific regulatory citations (§431.220, §431.221, §438.402, §438.406, §438.408) are supported by the Evidence block. The 90-day filing deadline for state fair hearings, the 60-day managed care appeal deadline, the one-level appeal requirement, clinical expertise requirements, and free case file provisions are all directly supported by the evidence. No hallucinations detected. The answer goes well beyond the reference answer in useful detail while remaining accurate, and a Medicaid policy expert would find it thorough and reliable.

items.question: Under the respiratory equipment policy (5A-2), can an adult beneficiary get a brand-new replacement CPAP machine every year?
items.answer:
No. An adult beneficiary cannot automatically get a brand-new replacement CPAP machine every year under Policy 5A-2. NC Medicaid uses established lifetime expectancies and quantity limits in Attachment A, Section C, and replacements before the usual life expectancy ends require a prior-approval request explaining why the replacement is needed. [Policy 5A-2 § 5.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5a-2-respiratory-equipment-and-supplies/download?attachment) [Policy 5A-2 § 5.9](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5a-2-respiratory-equipment-and-supplies/download?attachment)

The policy also says that, for purchased equipment, Medicaid may consider replacement when repair is no longer cost-effective and the item is out of warranty. [Policy 5A-2 § 5.9](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5a-2-respiratory-equipment-and-supplies/download?attachment) If the equipment can be repaired, the policy treats repair and service as the normal route, with repair covered for beneficiary-owned equipment when it is not under warranty. [Policy 5A-2 § 5.8](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5a-2-respiratory-equipment-and-supplies/download?attachment)

So the practical rule is: not every year just because a year has passed; replacement depends on the item’s listed lifetime expectancy and medical necessity, and early replacement needs specific justification. [Policy 5A-2 § 5.5](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5a-2-respiratory-equipment-and-supplies/download?attachment) [Policy 5A-2 § 5.9](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5a-2-respiratory-equipment-and-supplies/download?attachment)

I could verify that CPAP-related accessories in Attachment A, Section C have express yearly or monthly quantity limits, such as a combination oral/nasal mask at 4 per year and replacement cushions or nasal pillows at 2 per month, which reinforces that the policy manages this equipment by set limits rather than annual automatic full-machine replacement. [Policy 5A-2 Attachment A § C](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5a-2-respiratory-equipment-and-supplies/download?attachment)

I did not retrieve the full untruncated Attachment A row for the CPAP machine itself, so I could not verify the exact machine lifetime expectancy from the corpus text surfaced here. [Policy 5A-2 Attachment A § C](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5a-2-respiratory-equipment-and-supplies/download?attachment)

The current policy is the April 1, 2025 version, and the latest amendment notice says the 2025 revision was a throughout update for clarity and terminology consistency. [Policy 5A-2 Change Notice 2025-04-01](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5a-2-respiratory-equipment-and-supplies/download?attachment)

If you want, I can next try to pin down the exact lifetime expectancy for the CPAP machine HCPCS code in Attachment A, Section C.

items.question: Can a provider bill a telehealth visit under Policy 1-H for a general wellness check-in with no specific clinical indication?
items.answer:
**No—not based on Policy 1-H alone.** A general wellness “check-in” is not billable merely because it occurs by telehealth. The provider must bill an eligible underlying service within the provider’s licensed scope of practice, and the service must be one identified in Policy 1-H’s Attachment A or in the applicable program-specific clinical coverage policy. [Policy 1-H, Provider(s) Eligible to Bill for the Procedure, Product, or Service](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1h-telehealth-virtual-communications-and-remote-patient-monitoring/download?attachment) [Policy 1-H, Telehealth, Virtual Communications, and Remote Patient Monitoring Services Covered in Clinical Coverage Policy 1-H](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1h-telehealth-virtual-communications-and-remote-patient-monitoring/download?attachment) [Policy 1-H § 3.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1h-telehealth-virtual-communications-and-remote-patient-monitoring/download?attachment)

Policy 1-H allows telehealth delivery only when the provider determines that the particular service can be delivered **safely and effectively** for that beneficiary, considers the beneficiary’s abilities and safety, follows professional standards of care, obtains and documents consent, verifies identity, and protects privacy. [Policy 1-H § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1h-telehealth-virtual-communications-and-remote-patient-monitoring/download?attachment) A live telehealth visit also must use secure, HIPAA-compliant audio-video technology. [Policy 1-H § 5.3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1h-telehealth-virtual-communications-and-remote-patient-monitoring/download?attachment)

So, if “general wellness check-in” means there is no separately covered visit or service being provided and no beneficiary-specific basis showing that telehealth is appropriate, Policy 1-H does not support billing it as a telehealth encounter. The record should identify the actual covered service and support why telehealth was safe and effective for this beneficiary; telehealth-service documentation for medical services must also be sent to the identified primary care provider or medical home within 48 hours. [Policy 1-H § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1h-telehealth-virtual-communications-and-remote-patient-monitoring/download?attachment) [Policy 1-H § 7.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1h-telehealth-virtual-communications-and-remote-patient-monitoring/download?attachment)

The current Policy 1-H is effective February 1, 2025, and its documentation-and-billing section is marked amended February 15, 2025. [Clinical Coverage Policy 1-H](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1h-telehealth-virtual-communications-and-remote-patient-monitoring/download?attachment) [Policy 1-H § 7.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1h-telehealth-virtual-communications-and-remote-patient-monitoring/download?attachment)

items.question: Will NEMT take a beneficiary to the grocery store or other errands that aren't medical appointments?
items.answer:
No. NEMT is for trips whose **primary purpose is medical care** and that are for a Medicaid-covered service; a grocery-store trip or other personal errand does not meet that purpose. [Policy MA-2910 § IV.A, Medicaid Covered Services](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/MA-2910-.pdf)

More specifically, Medicaid pays NEMT to the nearest appropriate medical provider for a Medicaid-covered service furnished by an NC-enrolled Medicaid provider, using the least expensive appropriate transportation method. [Policy MA-2910 § II.A, Medicaid only pays for transportation](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/MA-2910-.pdf) Transportation requests and approvals are likewise for medical-service trips and medical appointments. [Policy MA-2910 § IX.A, Transportation Requests](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/MA-2910-.pdf) [Policy MA-2910 § IX.A, Types of Approvals](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/MA-2910-.pdf)

The agency may ask how someone gets to the store as part of deciding whether the person has other transportation resources for **medical appointments**; that assessment question does not make shopping transportation a covered NEMT trip. [Policy MA-2910 § VIII.C, Completing the assessment](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/MA-2910-.pdf)

The currently authoritative 2026 change notice updates NEMT per-diem and mileage-rate charts, not this medical-purpose limitation. [Policy MA-2910 Change Notice 04-26](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/CN-04-26-ABD.docx.pdf)

judge.explanation: The agent's answer correctly states that NEMT is limited to trips whose primary purpose is medical care for Medicaid-covered services, and that grocery/errand trips are not covered. This aligns with the reference answer and is directly supported by MA-2910 §IV.A and §II.A in the evidence. The agent provides accurate additional detail about the 'primary purpose' requirement, the nearest appropriate provider rule, and the assessment question about store trips (correctly noting it doesn't make shopping a covered NEMT trip). The amendment note about rate chart updates is supported by the getAmendments evidence. All citations reference MA-2910 sections that appear in the evidence. No hallucinated facts are present. The answer is more detailed than the reference but fully accurate and well-cited.

items.question: Does the CAP/DA waiver pay for rent, utilities, or food — that is, room and board — for a participant living in their own home?
items.answer:
**No—CAP/DA does not pay a participant’s ordinary room-and-board expenses, such as rent or utilities, for living in their own home.** The waiver’s covered services must be listed in the person-centered service plan, and the policy’s listed services and goods-and-services benefit do not include ongoing housing costs or utility bills. [Policy 3K-2 § 5.4.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) [Policy 3K-2 Appendix B, Goods and Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

**Food is different in a narrow way:** CAP/DA can cover *meal preparation and delivery* for someone assessed as needing special nutritional-planning assistance. That benefit is limited to **one nutritious meal per day** delivered to the person’s home, and may include a qualifying home meal through a delivery service or similar source. It is not a general grocery, food, or room-and-board allowance. [Policy 3K-2 § 3.4.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) [Policy 3K-2 Appendix B, Meal Preparation and Delivery](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) [Policy 3K-2 Appendix B, Meal Preparation and Delivery—Limits, Amount and Frequency](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

The current Policy 3K-2 is effective September 1, 2025; its associated revision notice states that the CAP/DA waiver renewal was CMS-approved effective November 1, 2024. [Policy 3K-2 Change Notice 2025-09-01](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

judge.explanation: The agent's answer is accurate and well-supported by the evidence. It correctly states that CAP/DA does not pay for rent or utilities, and correctly distinguishes the meal preparation/delivery benefit (one nutritious meal per day, Meals on Wheels style) from general food/grocery coverage. All key claims are supported by the evidence: Section 3.4.3 confirms meal preparation and delivery covers one nutritious meal per day; the Appendix B MEAL PREPARATION AND DELIVERY section confirms it can cover home meal delivery services like Uber Eats/DoorDash; the Limits section confirms one meal per day. The agent correctly notes the federal HCBS waiver design excludes room and board. No hallucinations detected - all claims are grounded in the evidence provided.

items.question: Can an adult who does not meet the medical-complexity criteria still receive private-duty nursing under NC Medicaid Policy 3G-1?
items.answer:
**No.** For adults, Policy 3G-1 requires the beneficiary to meet the policy’s health criteria in § 3.3, in addition to medical-necessity, eligibility, physician-order, prior-approval, residence, and trained-informal-caregiver requirements. [Policy 3G-1 § 3.2.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment) [Policy 3G-1 § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)

The Level 1 health criteria are the policy’s medical-complexity gateway: the adult must be ventilator-dependent for at least eight hours daily **or** satisfy the listed alternative criteria, including the required respiratory and skilled-nursing-intervention components. [Policy 3G-1 § 3.3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment) Level 2 services require meeting **all** Level 1 requirements plus an additional listed condition. [Policy 3G-1 § 3.3.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)

Policy 3G-1 expressly says Medicaid does **not** cover PDN when the beneficiary fails to meet the criteria in § 3.0. [Policy 3G-1 § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment) Also, care consisting only of observation or monitoring in case an intervention might become necessary is not “complex” skilled nursing and is not covered as medically necessary PDN. [Policy 3G-1 § 1.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)

judge.explanation: The agent's answer correctly states that adults must meet health criteria in § 3.3 to receive PDN under Policy 3G-1, accurately describes the Level 1 and Level 2 criteria including ventilator dependence and alternative criteria, correctly cites § 4.1 for the non-coverage rule when criteria in § 3.0 are not met, and correctly cites § 1.1.4 for the definition of 'complex' skilled nursing. All claims are directly supported by the Evidence block. Citations are precise and section-level. The answer is thorough and would be accepted by a Medicaid policy expert.

items.question: If a beneficiary buys an over-the-counter medication without a prescription for it, will NC Medicaid cover the cost?
items.answer:
**No—not if the beneficiary simply buys the OTC medication without a prescription.** Policy 9A § 1.0 NC Medicaid covers only selected OTC products, and the product must be dispensed by a pharmacist pursuant to a lawful prescription; it also must be on the covered OTC list and meet the other policy requirements. Policy 9A § 1.0

The covered OTC categories include, for example, certain nicotine products, proton-pump inhibitors, second-generation antihistamines, insulin and diabetes supplies, levonorgestrel emergency contraception, polyethylene glycol 3350, and OTC naloxone—but being on that list does not remove the prescription requirement. Policy 9A Attachment B

NC Medicaid’s outpatient pharmacy policy likewise says that selected OTC products are covered only when they meet Policy 9A’s criteria, and that the prescription must be written for the person whose claim is billed. [Policy 9 § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment) The policy was amended effective December 15, 2023 to add OTC naloxone to the covered list. Policy 9A Change Notice 2023-12-15

items.question: For grants administration applied to Medicaid, is 45 CFR Part 74 still the operative regulation, or has 45 CFR Part 75 replaced it?
items.answer:
**Neither 45 CFR Part 74 nor 45 CFR Part 75 is the current operative grants-administration regulation for Medicaid.** Part 74 was replaced by Part 75 when HHS implemented the Uniform Guidance in 2014, but HHS later rescinded Part 75 as well. Since October 1, 2025, the governing Uniform Guidance is **2 CFR Part 200**; both 45 CFR Parts 74 and 75 are reserved. [45 CFR Part 74](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/part-74) [45 CFR Part 75](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/part-75) [2 CFR Part 200](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-2/part-200)

### Medicaid-specific rule

For Medicaid grants to states, **42 CFR § 430.30(e) expressly applies 2 CFR Parts 200 and 300**, subject to two stated exceptions: 2 CFR § 200.306 (cost sharing/matching) and § 200.328 (financial reporting). [42 CFR § 430.30(e) (last revised 2024-10-02)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-430)

Thus, for a current Medicaid grants-administration analysis, cite **42 CFR § 430.30(e)** together with the pertinent provision of **2 CFR Part 200**, rather than either 45 CFR Part 74 or Part 75. The current Medicaid provision’s most recent listed Federal Register amendment is **89 FR 80069 (Oct. 2, 2024)**. [42 CFR § 430.30 (last revised 2024-10-02)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-430)

### Governing federal grants rule

Part 200 directs the federal agency or pass-through entity to select the appropriate federal-award instrument—such as a grant, cooperative agreement, subaward, or contract—under the Uniform Guidance. [2 CFR § 200.201](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-2/part-200)

### Practical citation

- **Current:** *42 CFR § 430.30(e); 2 CFR Part 200* (and, where relevant, 2 CFR Part 300). [42 CFR § 430.30(e) (last revised 2024-10-02)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-430)  
- **Historical only:** *45 CFR Part 74* for the pre-2014 HHS framework; *45 CFR Part 75* for the 2014–September 2025 HHS-specific Uniform Guidance framework. [45 CFR Part 74](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/part-74) [45 CFR Part 75](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-45/part-75)

judge.explanation: The agent's answer is fully accurate and complete. It correctly states that neither 45 CFR Part 74 nor Part 75 is operative, explains the historical supersession chain (74→75→reserved), identifies 2 CFR Part 200 as the current governing authority, and correctly cites 42 CFR § 430.30(e) as the Medicaid-specific cross-reference including the two exceptions (§ 200.306 cost sharing and § 200.328 financial reporting). All claims are supported by the Evidence block, including the amendment date of 89 FR 80069 (Oct. 2, 2024), the superseded status of both 45 CFR parts, and the current status of 2 CFR Part 200. The mention of 2 CFR Part 300 alongside Part 200 is also consistent with the text of 42 CFR § 430.30(e) shown in evidence. No hallucinations detected. Citations are precise and section-level throughout.

items.question: Have any amendments been made to the CAP/DA waiver policy since 2024?
items.answer:
**Yes.** The CAP/DA clinical policy, **Policy 3K-2**, has been amended since 2024. Its latest revision is dated **September 1, 2025**; NC Medicaid identifies that revision as applying to **all sections and attachments** and as the current authoritative amendment. [Policy 3K-2 Revision — 2025-09-01 (All sections and attachments)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

### Main current amendment
The September 1, 2025 revision implements CMS’s approved CAP/DA waiver renewal, which was effective **November 1, 2024**. [Policy 3K-2 Revision — 2025-09-01 (All sections and attachments)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

Among other changes, the revision:
- added the **CAP In-Home Aide II** service level throughout the policy; [Policy 3K-2 Revision — 2025-09-01 (All sections and attachments)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- removed medication-dispensing boxes as a standalone specialized-medical-supplies service, while allowing their purchase through the goods-and-services benefit; [Policy 3K-2 Revision — 2025-09-01 (Section 3.4.7)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- revised emergency-disaster-planning language and incident-reporting rules; [Policy 3K-2 Revision — 2025-09-01 (Section 7.4)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) [Policy 3K-2 Revision — 2025-09-01 (Section 7.5)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)
- revised paid-caregiver eligibility language related to felony convictions connected to health-care fraud; [Policy 3K-2 Revision — 2025-09-01 (6.5.12e)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) and
- updated claims-related material to add codes for CAP In-Home Aide II and In-Home Aide II–Respite. [Policy 3K-2 Revision — 2025-09-01 (Attachment A)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

There was also a separate **November 15, 2024** policy revision, including updates concerning eligibility, prior-approval procedures, service planning, provider requirements, and Appendix B service definitions. [Policy 3K-2 Revision — 2024-11-15 (2.0)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) [Policy 3K-2 Revision — 2024-11-15 (Appendix B)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

items.question: As it bears on HCBS waiver applications, what is the most recent change made to 42 CFR Part 441?
items.answer:
The most recent revision affecting HCBS waiver applications was CMS’s **May 10, 2024** update to the § 1915(c) HCBS rules in 42 CFR Part 441 (with compliance dates that begin to run from July 9, 2024 for several new requirements). The core application rule in § 441.301 was last revised in that rulemaking, **89 FR 40863 (May 10, 2024)**. [42 CFR § 441.301 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

## What changed for a § 1915(c) HCBS waiver application

A State’s waiver request still must include the § 441.302 assurances and § 441.303 supporting documentation, address any requested waivers of statewideness, comparability, or certain medically-needy financial rules, and state whether it will deny HCBS where expected HCBS costs exceed the comparable institutional level of care. [42 CFR § 441.301 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

The application must also show that services will be delivered under an agency-approved, written person-centered service plan; only to people who are not hospital, nursing-facility, or ICF/IID inpatients and who would otherwise need the applicable Medicaid-covered institutional level of care; and to defined target group(s). It must separately define each service and identify the qualifications of those who develop plans of care. [42 CFR § 441.301 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

The application/documentation package must substantiate health-and-welfare safeguards, financial accountability, beneficiary evaluation and regular reevaluation procedures, informed choice between institutional care and HCBS, applicable post-eligibility income/resource treatment, and cost-neutrality estimates. [42 CFR § 441.303 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

## Principal 2024 addition: new operational assurances and reporting

The substantive 2024 change was not a replacement of the basic waiver-application contents. It added extensive **incident-management, access, workforce, quality-measure, and public-reporting obligations** that a State must be prepared to assure and document as part of operating a § 1915(c) waiver. For example, the State must operate an incident-management system that identifies, reports, triages, investigates, resolves, tracks, and trends critical incidents; demonstrate specified minimum investigation and corrective-action performance; and report system-assessment results to CMS every **24 months**, unless CMS permits reporting no less often than every **60 months** for a compliant system. [42 CFR § 441.302 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441) [42 CFR § 441.311 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

The 2024 rule also requires annual reporting on critical incidents, person-centered planning reassessments and resulting plan updates, and the waiver’s impact on the type, amount, and cost of State-plan services; it further requires biennial reporting on the federal HCBS Quality Measure Set. [42 CFR § 441.311 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

## Timing and a technical later revision

The principal Part 441 HCBS amendments were published at **89 FR 40863–40871 (May 10, 2024)**. The incident-management requirements generally apply **three years after July 9, 2024**, while the electronic incident-data-system requirement generally applies **five years after July 9, 2024**. [42 CFR § 441.302 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

There was a later **June 27, 2024** Federal Register revision to § 441.312, the HCBS Quality Measure Set provision, cited at **89 FR 53502**; that is the latest section-level revision surfaced in Part 441, but it concerns quality-measure-set administration rather than changing the basic contents of a § 1915(c) waiver application. [42 CFR § 441.312 (last revised 2024-06-27)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

This is federal authority; whether and how North Carolina has incorporated these requirements into a particular waiver application or renewal is a separate NC implementation question.

---

The agent also correctly identifies both the older (441.301-441.303) and newer section numbering (441.311-441.313). items.question: Where in the federal regulations is the authority for 1915(c) home- and community-based services waivers like CAP/DA?
items.answer:
The federal **regulatory** authority for a § 1915(c) HCBS waiver—such as North Carolina’s CAP/DA waiver—is **42 C.F.R. Part 441, Subpart G**, especially **§§ 441.300–441.310**. The key provision is **42 C.F.R. § 441.300**, which states that § 1915(c) permits states to offer, through a waiver, home- and community-based services needed to avoid institutionalization. [42 CFR § 441.300](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

For a pinpoint citation on waiver eligibility and service-plan requirements, use **42 C.F.R. § 441.301(b)**: services must be furnished under a written person-centered service plan and only to a beneficiary whom the state determines would otherwise require the Medicaid-covered level of hospital, nursing-facility, or ICF/IID care. [42 CFR § 441.301 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

The underlying **statutory** authority—not a regulation—is **Social Security Act § 1915(c), 42 U.S.C. § 1396n(c)**. It authorizes the Secretary to waive specified Medicaid state-plan requirements so a state may cover approved HCBS, other than room and board, under a written plan of care for people who otherwise would need institutional-level care. [SSA § 1915(c)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)

For the regulatory definition of HCBS waiver services, see **42 C.F.R. § 440.180**, which cross-references Part 441, Subpart G.

judge.explanation: The agent's answer correctly identifies all key elements: the statutory authority (SSA § 1915(c), 42 USC § 1396n(c)), the implementing regulations in 42 CFR Part 441, Subpart G (§§ 441.300-441.310), and the cross-reference to 42 CFR § 440.180 for HCBS definitions. The agent correctly cites § 441.300 as the basis/purpose provision and § 441.301(b) for waiver eligibility and service-plan requirements, which aligns with the evidence showing § 441.300 states 'Section 1915(c) of the Act permits States to offer, under a waiver of statutory requirements, an array of home and community-based services.' The agent also correctly identifies § 441.302 (assurances) and § 441.303 (supporting documentation) implicitly through its discussion, and explicitly mentions § 441.301. The answer correctly distinguishes between statutory and regulatory authority. All claims are supported by the evidence blocks provided. The answer is comprehensive, well-cited, and accurate.

items.question: Which federal regulation sets the timeliness rules for amendments to a state's Medicaid plan (SPAs)?
items.answer:
The principal federal regulation is **42 C.F.R. § 430.12(c), “Plan amendments.”** [42 CFR § 430.12(c)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-430) It requires a state Medicaid plan to be amended when needed to reflect changes in federal law, regulations, policy interpretations, court decisions, or material state-law, organizational, policy, or operational changes; it also requires **prompt submission** so CMS can determine continued approvability and federal financial participation remains available. [42 CFR § 430.12(c) (last revised 2016-11-30)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-430)

For the SPA’s **effective date for federal financial participation**, use **42 C.F.R. § 430.20**: certain benefit, payment-increase, and eligibility-expansion amendments generally cannot be effective before the first day of the quarter in which an approvable amendment is submitted, while other amendments may use a CMS-approved state-requested effective date. [42 CFR § 430.20 (last revised 1991-03-01)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-430)

One important clarification: § 430.12 does **not** establish a general 60-day CMS review deadline for SPAs. Its express 60-day filing rule is limited to amendments concerning changes in state law on **advance directives**. [42 CFR § 430.12(c) (last revised 2016-11-30)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-430)

judge.explanation: The agent's answer correctly identifies 42 CFR § 430.12(c) as the primary regulation governing SPA amendments, accurately describes its requirements (prompt submission, triggers for amendment), correctly notes the 60-day rule is limited to advance directive changes, and properly references § 430.20 for FFP effective date rules. All claims are supported by the Evidence block. The answer adds useful nuance by clarifying what the 60-day rule does and does not cover, which is accurate per the evidence. Citations are precise to the section and paragraph level.

items.question: Point me to the federal rule that imposes medical loss ratio requirements on Medicaid managed care contracts.
items.answer:
The core federal MLR rule is **42 C.F.R. § 438.8**. It requires the state to ensure **through its Medicaid managed-care contracts** that every MCO, PIHP, and PAHP calculates and reports an MLR under the regulation’s methodology. [42 CFR § 438.8 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

A state is **not federally required to impose a minimum MLR in every contract**. But if it elects to require one, the contractual minimum must be **at least 85 percent**; each plan must calculate and report its MLR for each reporting year. [42 CFR § 438.8 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

The calculation is the ratio of a defined **numerator** to a defined **denominator**, with a possible credibility adjustment. The numerator generally includes incurred claims, qualifying health-care-quality-improvement expenditures, and fraud-prevention activities. [42 CFR § 438.8 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

For state oversight, **42 C.F.R. § 438.74** requires the state annually to submit CMS a summary of each contracted plan’s MLR report with the rate certification, including the numerator, denominator, achieved MLR, member months, and remittances owed. If the state’s contract requires remittances for missing the state-imposed minimum MLR, the state must repay CMS the federal share of those remittances. [42 CFR § 438.74 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

The most recent revision to § 438.8 was published at **89 FR 41272 (May 10, 2024)**, and the most recent revision to § 438.74 at **89 FR 41276 (May 10, 2024)**. [42 CFR § 438.8 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438) [42 CFR § 438.74 (last revised 2024-05-10)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

---

*Suggested citations for uncited claims above:*
- [42 CFR § 438.8(d)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

judge.explanation: The agent correctly identifies 42 CFR § 438.8 as the primary federal rule imposing MLR requirements on Medicaid managed care contracts, accurately describes the 85% minimum threshold (when states elect to mandate one), the calculation methodology (numerator/denominator with credibility adjustment), and the scope (MCOs, PIHPs, PAHPs). The agent also correctly cites § 438.74 for state oversight and CMS reporting requirements. The nuance about states not being federally required to impose a minimum MLR but needing to meet 85% if they do is accurate per § 438.8(c). All Federal Register citations (89 FR 41272 and 89 FR 41276, May 10, 2024) are supported by the evidence. No hallucinations detected - all claims are grounded in the evidence provided.

items.question: What is the federal authority establishing the EPSDT benefit for children on Medicaid?
items.answer:
The core federal authority is **Title XIX of the Social Security Act**.

- ** SSA § 1902(a)(43), 42 U.S.C. § 1396a(a)(43),** requires state Medicaid plans to provide EPSDT services for eligible individuals under age 21, arrange corrective treatment identified through screening, and inform families about the benefit. ** SSA § 1905(a)(4)(B), 42 U.S.C. § 1396d(a)(4)(B),** includes EPSDT within Medicaid “medical assistance.” [SSA § 1937(a)(1)(A)(ii), (E)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)

- ** SSA § 1905(r), 42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r),** defines EPSDT to include periodic screening; vision, dental, and hearing services; and other necessary health care, diagnostic services, treatment, and measures to “correct or ameliorate” conditions found through screening—**whether or not the service is otherwise covered under the state plan.** [SSA § 1905(r)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)

- For children enrolled in an Alternative Benefit Plan, ** 42 C.F.R. § 440.345(a)** requires the state to assure access to the **full EPSDT benefit** for any eligible child under 21, including through additional benefits if the benchmark package itself does not supply them. [42 CFR § 440.345 (last revised 2013-07-15)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

In short, the usual citation for the federal EPSDT entitlement is ** 42 U.S.C. §§ 1396a(a)(43) and 1396d(r)**—Social Security Act §§ 1902(a)(43) and 1905(r).

---

- [Section 1905(a)](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)
- [Section 1905(r). Early and periodic screening, diagnostic, and treatment services](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-chapter7-subchapter19)

items.question: Which federal regulation requires states to screen providers when they enroll in Medicaid?
items.answer:
The core regulation is **42 C.F.R. § 455.410(a)**. It requires each state Medicaid agency to require **all enrolled providers** to be screened under the provider-screening rules in 42 C.F.R. Part 455, Subpart E. [42 CFR § 455.410 (last revised 2021-08-13)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-455)

For **initial enrollment, re-enrollment, and revalidation**, **42 C.F.R. § 455.450** specifies that states must screen applications under a risk-based system—limited, moderate, or high—and apply the highest applicable risk level. [42 CFR § 455.450](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-455)

At the limited level, screening includes verifying applicable requirements, verifying licenses, and conducting specified database checks; moderate-risk providers also require site visits, while high-risk providers also require criminal-background checks and fingerprints. [42 CFR § 455.450](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-455)

---

- [42 CFR § 455.410](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-455)
